# Explain Like I’m 5 or Whatever I Choose: Evaluating the Potential for Interactive Complexity in Language Model Responses

**Authors:** Indu Panigrahi Tal August Affiliation: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Affiliation: {indup2, taugust}@illinois.edu

## Abstract

Given the increased use of large language models (LLMs) for reading and seeking information and the varying needs and backgrounds of users, direct manipulation of text can be a valuable mechanism for end-user control. However, enabling direct manipulation requires that models generate text consistent with user-requested changes. We focus on one such setting, manipulating the complexity of scientific information, and ask if models can generate multiple summaries along a continuum of text complexity that enable effective user selection and control. Through a within-subjects user study, we identify reliable complexity measures and a criterion for how models should conform to these measures. We evaluate five LLMs of different families, sizes, and reasoning abilities on $557$ scientific queries. We find that while models can vary complexity across responses, most changes remain inconsistent, with models shifting the complexity measures in the correct direction at most $33.67\%$ of the time.

## 1 Introduction

Scientists and students are increasingly using LLMs for reading (Fok et al., 2023; Lo et al., 2023) and synthesizing literature (Asai et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2025). Readers vary in their preferred responses based on their background (e.g., a junior vs. senior researcher) and context (e.g., reading within a familiar topic vs. new discipline), preferring simpler or more complex summaries and explanations (Guo et al., 2021; August et al., 2022; Joshi et al., 2025).

Past evaluations have focused on models’ ability to generate responses that align with different envisioned audiences (Joshi et al., 2025), or personalize a response to a given user (Guo et al., 2024b; Murthy et al., 2022). However, a single response can be misaligned with a user or fail to incorporate correct context (Gu et al., 2024). Further, responses may be inherently insufficient even if correct (Fok et al., 2024). For example, the design paradigm of details on demand (Min et al., 2025) suggests that users may—after seeing an initial summary—want more details, even if they did not want a detailed first response. While users might request more details, repetitive prompting is time-intensive (Zamfirescu-Pereira et al., 2023). Direct manipulation of text (e.g., a slider for text complexity) can be a more effective mechanism for end-user control (Zhang et al., 2026).

From an evaluation standpoint, this requires a shift towards evaluating the quality of multiple responses and how they relate to each other, rather than of single responses Joshi et al. (2025); Murthy et al. (2022). Thus, rather than asking if models can generate a single best scientific summary, in this paper we ask if models can generate multiple summaries that enable effective user selection and control. Triangulating with prior work, we identify measures of language complexity through a within-subjects user study where participants ( $N=16$ ) explored unfamiliar STEM11 1 Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics topics using a prototype chat interface that enabled direct manipulation of response language complexity (Fig. 1). Using an existing scientific QA benchmark (Asai et al., 2026), we test $5$ models of different sizes, families, and reasoning capabilities (GPT-5.1, GPT-5 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5 $\pm$ Thinking, and DeepSeek-V3.1) by generating $5$ versions, at different levels of response complexity22 2 We label complexity levels in our prompt by using different envisioned audiences, similar to past work (Joshi et al., 2025; August et al., 2022), see Sec 3.1., of answers to $557$ scientific queries. We define model performance based on the relationship between versions of a response.

We find that while models are able to vary complexity across responses, most changes remain inconsistent. For example, one of the better-performing models, Claude Sonnet 4.5 + Thinking, increases complexity $17.35\%$ of the time across the five versions for an individual query (and at most $76.53\%$ of the time for a single transition between versions). Additionally, models increase complexity measures less consistently between higher complexity responses than between lower complexity responses (e.g., $80.61\%$ of the time between the first two versions reduces to $43.88\%$ between the last two versions for Claude Sonnet 4.5). In summary, our paper makes the following contributions:

- 1. A new evaluation approach that tests models’ ability to generate multiple versions of a response across a dimension of interest. We instantiate the framework for scientific information seeking and language complexity.

- 2. A suite of three complexity measures motivated from prior work and grounded to a user study with $16$ participants reading scientific literature in unfamiliar disciplines. To evaluate models, we define a criterion for the relationship of complexity measures between versions of a response, further justified with additional human validation.

- 3. Evaluation results from $5$ models showing that models often fail to reliably adjust complexity measures in the correct direction across versions. Our findings hold across models and when we shift the complexity levels.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 LLMs for Information-Seeking

With the rising capabilities of LLMs being able to quickly produce different versions of text (Kirk et al., 2024; August et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023a), many LLM-powered interfaces have been developed to help people search for papers (Mudd et al., 2025), skim papers (Fok et al., 2023), aggregate information across multiple documents (Singh et al., 2025; Whitfield and Hofmann, 2023), and understand content (August et al., 2023; Rust et al., 2025b; Fok et al., 2023; Rust et al., 2025a; Fok et al., 2024). A popular option has been conversation-based, question-answering systems, such as Elicit (Whitfield and Hofmann, 2023), ASTA (Singh et al., 2025), and OpenAI’s Deep Research (OpenAI, 2025).

### 2.2 Adapting LLM Responses to Users

There have been two primary ways to adapt LLM responses to users: interactivity (i.e., the user decides what to see) (Min et al., 2025; Sundar et al., 2010; Färber et al., 2025; Head et al., 2021) and personalization (i.e., the system decides what the user sees) (Kim et al., 2025b; Adar et al., 2017; August et al., 2022; Acharya et al., 2018). Past evaluations in complexity adaption have had an implicit personalization context, meaning the goal was for the model to generate a single correct response, evaluating whether or not LLMs could simplify text by generating a response at a 5th grade reading level when prompted with “explain like I am a 5th grader” for example (Beks van Raaij et al., 2024; Hedlin et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025; Färber et al., 2025). We instead focus on an interactive context by evaluating how well models generate a range of responses, allowing users to choose between levels of complexity. We explore this alternative framing because users may need to select their own version depending on their needs in the moment (Fok et al., 2024) rather than on a static attribute (e.g., a professor wanting a simple definition of a term in their field). While users can prompt models for this information, specifying information needs iteratively can be time-consuming and distracting (Zamfirescu-Pereira et al., 2023).

## 3 Formative User Study

Inspired by small-scale formative studies in Human-Computer Interaction research (Kim et al., 2023; Sauro and Lewis, 2012), and their growing use in NLP to identify a contextualized task of interest to then evaluate at scale (Guo et al., 2024b; Kim et al., 2023; Bhatt et al., 2025), we conduct a formative study with $16$ participants to structure our subsequent model evaluation (Sec. 4). Our formative study: (1) validates the utility of interactive complexity in the context of scientific information seeking, (2) corroborates characteristics of language associated with user-perceived complexity, and (3) identifies requirements for model responses that enable successful interactive complexity.

### 3.1 Study Design and Analysis

#### Procedure

We recruited $16$ participants to interact with two interfaces. An interactive complexity chat provided users with a slider mechanism to adjust the language complexity of responses, choosing from $5$ levels, $1$ being the least complex (Fig. 1). The conventional interface looked and functioned similar to a basic chat interface (i.e., without the slider). All studies were counterbalanced between the two interfaces.

To emulate the experience of exploring new, knowledge-intensive topics with the interfaces, we asked each participant to provide two STEM topics before the study that they had interest in but little to no knowledge about. For each interface, participants were instructed to identify facts and a paper within their chosen topics.

While interacting with each interface, participants actively verbalized their reasoning and impressions. After each condition, we interviewed participants about their experience with the interface. More details and materials are provided in Appendix A.5.

#### Response Generation

We used the participant-provided topics to generate scientific reports using a RAG-based pipeline (Singh et al., 2025, ScholarQA,) with Claude Sonnet 4.5. Using these reports as inputs, we prompted GPT-5 mini33 3 Chosen for low latency appropriate for an interactive context. to generate $5$ versions of the reports for audiences defined as College student, Junior Ph.D. student, Senior Ph.D. student, Postdoctoral researcher, and Senior researcher44 4 We based these levels off of previous work that stratifies model responses using level of education (Joshi et al., 2025; August et al., 2024), adjusting the levels to be appropriate for the envisioned prompts (i.e., scientific literature queries). to populate the slider. Appendix A.1 includes the prompt and describes alternative prompts we tested.

#### Analysis

To analyze the participant responses, we employ open coding (Saldaña, 2021) (details in Appendix A.5.6). Since all authors were on consultation for study coding, we did not calculate inter-rater reliability (McDonald et al., 2019). The codes describe participants’ sentiments (e.g., “Appreciates agency of interactive chat”) and interactions (e.g., “Prompted with desired complexity”).

*Figure 1: Interactive language complexity interface Users can manipulate textual complexity by moving the response slider (A) to a different notch. Sentences that are significantly different from those in the previously-displayed version are highlighted (B); significant differences are determined by comparing sentence-level BERTScores (Zhang et al., 2020) to a threshold. The preset default is 3, and there is an option to change the default to apply to all sliders.*

### 3.2 Results

#### Interactive complexity is valuable over a conventional chat interface

The majority of participants (13/16) appreciated the flexibility that interactive complexity provided beyond prompting. Participants found the responses from the conventional chat interface inconsistent in terms of complexity, sometimes providing too much or too little information or jargon (13/16). In fact, seven participants (four of whom had not yet seen the interactive condition) ended up describing their preferred level of complexity in follow-up prompts, indicating a strong desire for control over perceived complexity of responses.

#### Jargon, information, and length influenced perceived complexity

As participants decreased complexity, they prioritized three primary, desired trends: decreases in scientific jargon (16/16), amount of information (13/16), and length (12/16). This finding reinforces what prior work has proposed for measuring complexity (August et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024a) and forefronts the measures that we focus on in our model evaluation (Sec. 4).

#### Small changes in complexity are hard to perceive

While five levels of complexity seemed generally appropriate (10/16), ten participants noted the levels needed to be more distinct from each other. In particular, six participants shared the sentiment that P9 expressed of “one and two [the least complex versions] and four and five [didn’t] feel all that much different”. This observation suggests that some responses did not strictly increase in complexity, conflicting with what users expect and need.

## 4 Evaluating Interactive Complexity

Motivated by our formative findings, we test the potential for models to provide responses that enable interactive complexity. Below we describe the data (Sec. 4.1) and models (Sec. 4.2) used in our evaluation, as well as our measures of complexity (Sec. 4.3) and our criterion to facilitate effective user control over model responses (Sec. 4.4).

### 4.1 Scientific Query Data

We use $557$ queries from ScholarQABench (Asai et al., 2026) which contains expert-written scientific queries across multiple STEM fields (Appendix A.2.1). $98$ of these queries come with expert-written answer reports. We restrict one evaluation to this subset to use the expert-written reports for grounding model responses to a single ground truth report (similar to the user study); this choice aligns with past work on the utility of human-written context (Tan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023) and potential issues with reusing models for both initial ground truth generation and subsequent response generation (Xu et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2024). Since this restriction leads to a relatively small sample, we run a second evaluation on a larger sample of queries from the rest of ScholarQABench with reports generated from ScholarQA (Singh et al., 2025), similar to the user study. Specifically, we randomly sample $500$ scientific queries from ScholarQABench (excluding the aforementioned $98$ ) and generate a report for each using the ScholarQA pipeline (Singh et al., 2025) with a Claude Sonnet 4.5 backend. We use these reports as inputs to each model. We report results on $459$ queries due to model refusal on some of the queries.

### 4.2 Models

We prompt models the same way as for the user study (Sec. 3.1)—to generate $5$ versions of the input, stratified for five envisioned audiences going from least to most complex (College student $\rightarrow$ Senior researcher). Since we label each version with an intended audience, we run a third evaluation that uses alternative audience labels (Child $\rightarrow$ Expert) (Sec. 5.4). We evaluate $5$ models across different sizes, model families, and reasoning abilities: GPT-5.1, GPT-5 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (with and without Thinking), and DeepSeek-V3.1. Details about model configurations are in Appendix A.3.

### 4.3 Complexity Measures

Past work has quantified complexity through several linguistic measures. These include readability formulas Flesch (1948), lexical features, and perplexity measures (Guo et al., 2024a; August et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2025). We triangulate between these works and our formative study results (Sec. 3.2) to curate a suite of three measures,55 5 The Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease Score Flesch (1948) is a commonly-used scale for rating complexity; however, past work has shown that Flesch-Kincaid scores do not provide a reliable measure of complexity Cachola et al. (2025). We focus on the measures confirmed in our user study and provide Flesch-Kincaid data (reflects similar trends as the other measures) in Appendix A.4.1. each representing different dimensions of perceived language complexity:

- • Jargon Guo et al. (2024a); Joshi et al. (2025): This measure denotes the number of words that are considered specialized or technical. We calculate the percentage of words in the response that are not on the Dale-Chall Word List, a list of $3{,}000$ familiar English words (Chall and Dale, 1995).

- • Information Trienes et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2024a): More complex language often includes more information (e.g., technical details). We query GPT-4.1 to identify the number of independent facts, using the pipeline for generating “atomic facts” from Min et al. (2023); we validate the performance by manually inspecting a subset of $25$ examples (Appendix A.6.1).

- • Length (Joshi et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024a): More complex language, similar to containing more information, is often longer. However, simpler language can also be longer when the same information is explained or elaborated66 6 We consider information density (the ratio between Information and Length) as way to measure elaborative simplification. However, we already include both measures separately, and model performance was lower than and reflected the same trends as with our selected measures (Appendix A.4.2) on (Wu et al., 2023b). We quantify length as the total number of response characters.

### 4.4 Criterion for effective user control

Based on prior work (Guo et al., 2024a; Joshi et al., 2025; August et al., 2024) and our formative user study, we define model performance as a model’s ability to increase complexity measures as the intended complexity levels increase. We operationalize this by evaluating the direction of changes in the complexity measures across the $5$ versions of a response. Models that are better at generating distinct levels of complexity will produce positive changes in all measures.

Our criterion rests on the assumption that our measures of complexity capture a user’s perception of complexity. To validate this assumption, we perform a comparison between the complexity measures and human ratings of perceived complexity. We randomly sampled $100$ pairs of generated text from consecutive levels in our model evaluation (evenly sampled across the four transitions and five models) and conducted manual binary comparisons of which text was perceived as more complex. Comparisons were done by two authors in the research team in a blind setting77 7 The texts within each sampled pair were shuffled, and two authors rated the first $25$ pairs. Since the authors achieved high agreement ( $88\%$ , Cohen’s $\kappa$ = $0.75$ ), one author rated the remaining $75$ pairs.. Importantly, ratings were not focused on measuring Jargon, Information, or Length, but rather a user’s overall perceived complexity. We compare agreement, measured as Cohen’s $\kappa$ 88 8 Chosen for two raters classifying samples according to a binary category., between these human ratings and the complexity measures (Tab. 1). We find that the agreement between the ratings and the combination of all measures is substantial ( $\kappa=0.84$ ), and much higher than any single measure alone (e.g., Jargon alone is $\kappa=0.56$ ). This further emphasizes the importance of all measures increasing together as opposed to individually.

### 5.1 Models inconsistently increase complexity measures

Models often increase the complexity for some inputs while decreasing the complexity for others for the same transition. In Fig. 2, this can be seen where distributions cover positive and negative changes for the same model and transition, particularly in Jargon and Information. For example, when transitioning from Level 3 to 4, Claude Sonnet 4.5 + Thinking increases all three measures for only $58.16\%$ of the expert-written inputs ( $48.58\%$ for model-generated inputs) (Tab. 2). Fig. 4 shows an example where Jargon and Information both decrease when the complexity is supposed to increase. Length often moves in the correct direction; however, as shown by our criterion, all measures should move in the correct direction together (discussed further in Sec. 5.2).

When considering all transitions (Tab. 3), Claude Sonnet 4.5 + Thinking is the best-performing but only consistently increases complexity measures $17.35\%$ of the time ( $4.79\%$ for generated inputs). Our significance tests further show that for Jargon and Information, the mean of changes moving in the wrong direction is often significantly different from those moving in the right direction ( $p<0.01$ for expert-written and generated inputs), implying responses that fail to increase in complexity instead significantly decrease in complexity (as opposed to having no significant difference) (Appendix A.2.3).

The proportion of stagnant changes are at most $1.02\%$ for Jargon, $7.14\%$ for Information, and $0\%$ for Length; thus we focus the proportion of changes that decrease as a stronger indication of complexity going in the wrong direction.

### 5.2 Models increase length with complexity

Unlike Jargon and Information, models generally increase Length with increasing complexity. This can be seen in Tab. 3 as all models increase Length across the $5$ levels for the majority of their inputs (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.1 increases Length across all levels $98.98\%$ of the time, $98.47\%$ for generated inputs), reflecting the per-transition performance in Tab. 2. However, an increase in Length alone may not always indicate an increase in complexity. When directly examining responses, we notice that cases where Length increases on its own (without increasing Jargon or Information) can be indicative of elaborative simplification Wu et al. (2023b); an example is shown in Fig. 3.

*Figure 3: Example of elaborative simplification Snippets of responses generated by Claude Sonnet 4.5 that are supposed to increase in complexity. Between the two, Length increases, while Jargon and Information decrease. The additional text in the Level 4 snippet explains in simple language the term “meta-reason” in the Level 3 snippet.*

*Figure 4: Example of text incorrectly decreasing in complexity Shown are two snippets of text generated by GPT-5.1 that are meant to increase in complexity from Level 2 to Level 3. However, we qualitatively observe that the complexity decreases between analogous phrases (e.g., “platform selection” from Level 3 reads simpler than “achieving robust, high-titer expression in suitable production platforms” from Level 2). Decreases in Jargon and Information reflect this observation; the measures represent the texts that the snippets are from, not the snippets in isolation, explaining why Length increases.*

### 5.3 Models struggle to differentiate responses in later audience levels

In addition to the overall performance discussed in the previous two findings, we consider how the performance varies by transition. We find that models increase complexity measures more often when transitioning from Level 1 to Level 2 than for the later transitions. This can be seen in Tab. 2 where most models have the highest percentage of inputs moving in the correct direction of complexity in the “1 to 2” row compared to the later rows. For example, GPT-5 mini correctly increases all measures for $62.25\%$ of the inputs when going from Level 1 to 2, which is higher than $42.86\%$ , $27.55\%$ , and $41.84\%$ for the later transitions.

### 5.4 Expanding audience labels can improve performance but exhibits the same trends

We chose the audiences ‘‘College student’’ through ‘‘Senior researcher’’ because the wording of the queries in ScholarQABench implies that the inquirer has at least a college education. We investigate if this choice of audience labels affects the similarity between levels by running an identical evaluation to the first using a different set of audience labels. Specifically, we use labels from a popular video series called ‘‘5 Levels’’ by WIRED99 9 https://www.wired.com/video/series/5-levels/ that focuses on communicating specialized concepts to $5$ different audiences: Child, Teen, College student, Grad student, and Expert.

While complexity measures increase more often (i.e., the percentages of responses moving in the correct direction are generally higher than those in the first evaluation, Tab. 3), the same trend of measures moving in the wrong direction holds. For example, the percent of inputs that Claude Sonnet 4.5 increases in complexity across all transitions improved from $14.29\%$ to $33.67\%$ with the change in audience labels (Tab. 3); however, $33.67\%$ remains relatively low.

In terms of per-transition performance (Tab. 2), the “Child $\rightarrow$ Expert” labels increase complexity measures more often than the “College $\rightarrow$ Senior researcher” labels in the first evaluation, suggesting that the model interprets the former as more distinct from each other. However, we observe the same trend where models differentiate between Levels 1 and 2 better than the later levels. This can be seen when the performance of GPT-5 mini decreases from $80.61\%$ in the first transition to $56.12\%$ in the last (Tab. 2). Similar to the first evaluation, our significance tests further imply that for Jargon and Information, responses that fail to increase in complexity often significantly decrease in complexity ( $p<0.01$ for expert-written and generated inputs) (Appendix A.2.3).

## 6 Discussion & Conclusion

Enabling users to directly adjust the language of model responses allows LLM-powered systems to better accommodate user needs. While prompting remains the default for adjusting model responses, new malleable interfaces promise more direct user control beyond articulating information needs through language (Min et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). In this paper, we propose an evaluation approach for these settings that tests multiple responses relative to each other rather than single responses in isolation. Through a formative user study and additional human validation, we establish that these interactive use cases can be desirable, specifically for controlling language complexity, and identify measures and a criterion for distinguishing between levels of complexity. To investigate how current models fulfill or stray from users’ expectations, we evaluate model-generated levels of complexity for answers to a dataset of scientific queries, varying the answer source and range of intended audiences. We show that evaluating models across levels of complexity reveals model weaknesses that would be difficult to identify in single-response evaluations. Specifically, models do not consistently increase complexity and that their performance can worsen for higher complexity levels. Further, while models tend to increase length with complexity levels, they frequently decrease jargon and information, suggesting that models often neglect attributes that are important for perceived complexity and end-user control.

Our evaluation approach has parallels with other recent trends in model evaluations, such as evaluating multi-turn conversations (Laban et al., 2026), integrated or live use settings (Mehta et al., 2026; Bragg et al., 2026), and performance measures based on different intended audiences (Joshi et al., 2025). More generally, as models are integrated into new interfaces (Joshi and Vogel, 2026; Lee et al., 2024, e.g., reading or writing interfaces,), evaluations must shift to incorporate interface-specific criteria.

## Limitations

We evaluated models using linguistic measures that were strongly supported by prior work and our formative study. However, there are other potential measures for complexity that could go beyond linguistic characteristics towards the content of the text, such as elaborative simplification and analogies. Thus, one avenue for future work would be to quantify and evaluate the impact of these additional measures, potentially with additional open-source LLMs as well to increase accessibility.

We structure our user study around the target setting of people learning unfamiliar scientific topics. While sample sizes for formative studies are often small Guo et al. (2024b); Kim et al. (2023); Sauro and Lewis (2012), we noticed the same salient comments and interactions among our participants, suggesting data saturation for readers in unfamiliar STEM fields. We recognize this is a focused subset of the broader audience of scientific papers; an interesting expansion would be to analyze text from other disciplines.

Lastly, there are also other options for interactivity to explore. For our evaluation, the model generates a full response for each of the five levels, and we test different prompting techniques for this (Appendix A.1). However, one could imagine, for example, an interface where users select a specific snippet of text to be rewritten into a different complexity, which leads to other possibilities for direct manipulation.

## Ethical Considerations

This work uses LLMs to generate and evaluate responses. In addition to their impact on the environment (Ren et al., 2024; Desislavov et al., 2023), LLMs can hallucinate and exhibit biases that affect the information they generate (Venkit et al., 2024; Sharma et al., 2024; Zhou and Di Eugenio, 2025). At the same time, we believe that the contribution of this work towards making information from knowledge-intensive domains accessible to people of varying expertise is valuable. Additionally, we focus on English text; however, this does not necessarily account for contexts with ESL learners who may have different experiences that impact scientific information seeking.

### A.4 Additional Measures

#### A.4.1 Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease Score Data

The Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease Score is a commonly-used scale for rating complexity (Flesch, 1948; Joshi et al., 2025; Ágústsdóttir et al., 2025; Färber et al., 2025). However, past work has shown that Flesch-Kincaid scores do not provide a reliable measure of complexity (Cachola et al., 2025; Tanprasert and Kauchak, 2021; Imperial and Tayyar Madabushi, 2023), and we found that our findings remain the same as the scores exhibit similar trends to Jargon and Information.

Fig. 6 shows the changes in Flesch-Kincaid scores across levels labeled with our initial audiences and the WIRED audiences. Flesch-Kincaid scores follow the opposite trend to the measures in the main paper; a decrease in the score indicates higher complexity. Similar to Jargon and Information (Fig. 2), we observe inconsistent increases in complexity (i.e., decreasing Flesch-Kincaid scores).

*Figure 6: Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease score data These plots show the distributions of changes in the Flesch-Kincaid scores between consecutive levels for the two sets of audience labels that we prompted with. Expert-written inputs were used for $n=98$ , and model-generated inputs were used for $n=459$ . Since a higher Flesch-Kincaid score means that the text is more readable, decreasing the scores as complexity increases is desirable.*

#### A.4.2 Information Density

Information is one of the three measures used in our evaluations. An alternative to providing the raw number of information points as we do for Information is to calculate the ratio between information and length. We test such a measure, using the number of sentences to represent length following the idea that a sentence can represent a single information point. The results are detailed in Tab. 13 as the percent of inputs moving in the correct direction at each transition, similar to Tab. 2. We find that model performance according to this measure is worse than according to the other measures, having fewer inputs moving in the correct direction per transition. Additionally, while we divide by the number of sentences, there is no standardized way to calculate information density.

### A.6 Validity checks

#### A.6.1 Manual validation of Information measure

We used the prompt provided by Min et al. (2023) for identifying what they call “atomic facts” (defined as “pieces of information”). Since we used a more recent model (GPT-4.1 instead of InstructGPT), we manually validated a randomly-sampled subset of $25$ responses according to the following procedure and achieved $80\%$ agreement between the Information measure and the human rater:

- 1. One author manually identified all atomic facts following the procedure and definition from Min et al. (2023).

- 2. The number of manually-identified facts was compared to the number of atomic facts that GPT-4.1 identified.

- 3. If the GPT-4.1 number was $\pm 2$ of the author’s number, it was considered consistent.

#### A.6.2 Factuality

We run an evaluation of factual correctness using SummaC Laban et al. (2022) to compare the model responses to the human-written reports that were used. SummaC is a popular NLI-based measure of how much a summary follows from a source; higher scores indicate that more of the information in the original report is retained and correct. We find that the responses have moderate scores, consistent across levels within the same model (Tab. 16). This suggests, unsurprisingly, that information is lost in text simplification and to a similar degree across levels.
